CAR-1 has also been found to sustain putative mutations, particularly in breast cancer, and methylation in colon cancer. Previous molecular analysis conducted on breast carcinoma cell lines has shown both heterozygous missense and intronic mutations in exon 2. Mutational analyses of exon 4 in breast tumor samples also show mutations, indicating a possible loss, decrease, or change of protein function.

Many RING finger proteins of the RBCC family form oncogenic fusion proteins linked to oncogenesis by functioning in either epigenetic silencing mechanisms or transcriptional repression. RING finger family proteins such as Breast Cancer 1 (BRCA-1), promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML), and Enhance of Polycomb (EPC) have been shown to form multi-protein complexes in cells. For instance, in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), the RBCC protein PML was seen as discrete, nuclear localized PML oncogenic domains (PODs). Since formation of PODs relies on fully functional RING domains, the RING may be important in protein-protein interactions. Such macromolecular complexes vary in size from the larger entities of PML to the smaller complexes of BRCA1. Evidence also indicates involvement of the RBCC domain in homo-oligomerization, which may function in the physical interaction of the various RING finger proteins.¹,²

Affinity-purified CAR-1 anti-peptide antibodies, targeted to the amino and carboxyl terminal regions of CAR-1, have been isolated. These antibodies will be utilized in immunocytochemistry and immunohistochemistry.

As part of a functional study of CAR-1 as a tumor suppressor, protein function and localization will be analyzed to characterize the normal function of CAR-1. Western blots, immunocytochemistry, and immunohistochemistry will be used to examine the role of specific CAR-1 domains in subcellular localization and the formation of macromolecular complexes. The results may substantiate CAR-1 as a tumor suppressor gene for histologically diverse cancers.

The samples, Kaleidoscope prestained standard marker (BioRad, Hercules, CA), and ECL protein molecular weight marker was loaded into a PAGEr Gold precast gel (12% with 12 lanes) (Cambex, Rockland, ME) and mounted in a EC120 mini vertical gel system with Tris-Glycine electrode buffer (125 mM Tris Base, 960 mM glycine, 0.5% SDS, and water).

Following electrophoresis, the gel soaked in transfer buffer (3.03 g Trizma Base, 14.4 g glycine, 200 ml methanol, water). A sheet of Hybond-P protein transfer membrane (Amersham, Piscataway, NJ) was prewet in 100% methanol, washed in distilled water, and equilibrated in transfer buffer. The gel and Hybond-P was set up in an electroblot system for protein transfer, which ran for 1.5 h. The protein blot was blocked overnight with 10 ml TBST and 5% Amersham blocking reagent at 4°C.

The membrane was washed with TBST and then incubated for one hour with rotation with primary antibody, CAR-1 Rb anti-7b5-Coil peptide (C-terminal peptide) (Bethyl Laboratories, Montgomery, TX) at 1:20,000. The membrane was then incubated with secondary antibody, goatarabbit HRP at 1:5000 and Streptavadin-HRP (Amersham) at 1:25,000 for one hour with rotation. The membrane was washed with the same series of TBST washes as before.
The membrane was then treated with an ECL plus Western Blotting Detection System and exposed to Hyperfilm ECL (Amersham).
